pairs.rationale: Both warn against Pharisaic leaven. Luke explicitly identifies it as hypocrisy; Matthew includes the Sadducees and does not use hypocrisy in this verse. The metaphor is not given one meaning in every context.
Both say covered things will be revealed and hidden things become known. Matthew uses the assurance against fear; Luke follows the hypocrisy warning.
Both contrast private speech in darkness with public speech in light and on rooftops. Luke predicts exposure of what hearers said; Matthew commands proclamation of Jesus' teaching.
Both forbid fearing people whose power reaches bodily death. Matthew also explicitly contrasts inability to kill the soul; Luke states their inability to do more after killing.
Both direct fear toward the one with power over Gehenna. Matthew explicitly names destruction of soul and body; Luke speaks of authority to cast there after death.
Both use cheap sparrows to illustrate God's care. Luke says five for two assaria and none forgotten; Matthew says two for one assarion and none falling apart from the Father.
Both join numbered hairs, greater value than sparrows, and freedom from fear. Matthew distributes the assurance across two verses.
Both connect public acknowledgment of Jesus with heavenly acknowledgment. Luke names the Son of Man before God's angels; Matthew names Jesus before His Father.
Both warn of heavenly denial following denial of Jesus before people. Luke names God's angels; Matthew names His Father as the heavenly audience.
Both distinguish forgivable speech against the Son of Man from unforgivable blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. Matthew adds neither in this age nor the coming one.
Both forbid advance anxiety about speech under hostile proceedings. Luke specifies synagogues, rulers, and authorities; Matthew speaks of being handed over and supplied words.
Both promise Spirit-given speech at the needed hour. Luke says the Holy Spirit teaches; Matthew says the Father's Spirit speaks in the disciples.

Both use the question who appointed someone judge. Luke has Jesus question the requested role of judge or divider; Exodus has a challenger question Moses' authority as ruler and judge. The roles and occasions differ.

Both reject treating possessions as life's security. Luke warns against greed; Timothy joins life's transience and contentment with warnings about destructive desire for riches. It does not narrate Luke's inheritance dispute.

Both introduce a wealthy figure in a warning about imagined security and uncertain remaining life. Luke's wealth comes from an abundant crop; Sirach describes attention and frugality, preserving different means of gain.

Both rich figures speak of rest and enjoying stored good things. Sirach immediately warns of unknown remaining time; Luke's speaker confidently imagines many years before the following divine interruption.
Both contrast accumulated goods with death and their passing to others. Luke specifies this night and asks whose the goods will be; Sirach gives no fixed night and says they are left to others.
Both contrast self-directed earthly accumulation with wealth oriented beyond it. Luke says rich toward God; Matthew contrasts vulnerable earthly treasure with heavenly treasure.
Both tell disciples not to worry over food or clothing for life and body. Matthew also mentions drinking in this verse; Luke does not.
Both reason that life is more than food and the body more than clothing. Matthew includes that reasoning with the initial anxiety prohibition.
Both contrast birds' lack of sowing and storage with God's feeding them and humans' greater value. Luke names ravens; Matthew refers generally to sky birds.
Both ask whether anxiety can add a cubit to a person's span of life. The unusual measurement image remains as supplied.

Both sequences move from anxiety's inability to alter life's measure to questioning further anxiety. Luke calls this the smallest thing and asks about the rest; Matthew turns specifically to clothing.
Both point to lilies that neither toil nor spin and surpass Solomon's clothing in glory. Matthew splits the observation and Solomon comparison into two verses.
Both reason from God's clothing grass, present today and burned tomorrow, to His greater care for people, addressing their little faith.
Both reject anxious preoccupation with eating and drinking. Matthew also names clothing; Luke adds not being unsettled.
Both contrast the nations' pursuit of necessities with the Father's knowledge of the disciples' need.
Both direct seeking God's kingdom with necessities added. Matthew explicitly includes His righteousness; Luke's supplied verse does not.
Both present the kingdom as a benefit from the Father. Luke reassures the little flock that He is pleased to give it; Matthew invites the Father's blessed to inherit the prepared kingdom.
Both direct attention to heavenly treasure safe from theft and moths. Luke explicitly adds selling possessions, almsgiving, and enduring purses; Matthew does not repeat those instructions here.
Both state that the heart will be where one's treasure is, explaining the preceding choice of treasure.

Both use prepared attendants and lamps in watchfulness teaching. Luke commands girded loins and burning lamps before a master's return; Matthew describes virgins with differing oil supplies before the bridegroom. The parables remain distinct.
Both portray servants and door duties awaiting an absent master. Luke specifies return from a wedding and opening promptly at a knock; Mark specifies travel abroad and an unknown return.
Both bless servants whom the returning master finds fulfilling their duty. Luke uniquely adds the master serving the watchful slaves; Matthew's verse does not supply that role reversal.
Both connect nighttime return with vigilance. Luke blesses those awake in second or third watches; Mark lists evening, midnight, cockcrow, and morning and warns against being found asleep.
Both use the householder who would prevent a burglary if he knew when the thief would come. Matthew explicitly mentions keeping watch and the watch of the night; Luke says hour.
Both require readiness because the Son of Man comes at an unexpected hour.

Peter asks whether the watchfulness parable addresses the disciples or everyone; Mark explicitly extends watchfulness from immediate hearers to all. Mark does not narrate Peter's question or serve as an identical answer in Luke's scene.
Both ask about a faithful, prudent servant appointed to distribute household food at the proper time. Luke calls him a steward and names grain rations.
Both bless the servant found carrying out his assigned responsibility when the master arrives.
Both promise appointment over all the master's possessions as the faithful servant's reward.
Both depict an assumed delay followed by violence against fellow servants and indulgence. Luke names male and female servants and drunkenness; Matthew names dining with drunkards.
Both describe unexpected return, cutting the slave in two, and assigning his portion with an excluded group. Luke names the unfaithful; Matthew names hypocrites and adds weeping and grinding teeth.
Both increase accountability through knowing the good but failing to act. Luke gives the informed slave many blows; James calls knowing omission sin without repeating that punishment scheme.

Both connect greater responsibility with stricter accountability. Luke says more is demanded from greater entrustment; James warns teachers of greater judgment, without repeating the ignorant slave's few blows.

Both associate the coming mission with fire. Matthew's John mentions Spirit-and-fire baptism and burning chaff; Luke's Jesus speaks of casting fire on earth. The image comparison does not decide a single meaning of Luke's fire.

Both have Jesus describe His coming experience as a baptism. Mark joins it with the cup and disciples' participation; Luke emphasizes constraint until accomplishment. No identical ritual or chronology is imposed.
Both deny uncomplicated earthly peace as the result of Jesus' coming. Luke says division; Matthew uses a sword image.
Both describe division within a household because of Jesus' mission. Luke specifies five divided three against two; Matthew supplies family pairings and household enemies without those numbers.
Both list father/son, mother/daughter, and mother-in-law/daughter-in-law divisions. Luke gives reciprocal directions; Matthew expresses the divisions in one direction.

Both contrast ordinary weather forecasting with failed discernment. Luke's indicator is a cloud rising in the west that signals rain; Matthew's is a red sky with fair or storm weather. The actual indicators are different.
Both cite recognizable weather signs. Luke names a south wind predicting heat; Matthew names red sky predicting fair weather or storm. Neither forecast is substituted for the other.
Both rebuke ability to assess sky appearances alongside inability to discern the present significant time or its signs. Luke names earth and sky; Matthew names sky and signs of the times.
Both call for right judgment. Luke asks why people do not judge what is right for themselves; John commands righteous judgment rather than judgment by appearance, in a different dispute.
Both urge settlement with an adversary on the way before a judge and officer lead to imprisonment. Luke frames it before a ruler; Matthew says come to terms quickly.
Both warn that release waits until the last small coin is paid. Luke names a lepton; Matthew a quadrans, preserving the distinct coins.

Both challenge an assumed direct inference from a person's suffering to particular guilt. Luke rejects the victims being greater sinners; John rejects the proposed sin explanation of congenital blindness, not a general claim that the family never sinned.
Both connect repentance with avoiding death. Ezekiel commands turning from impieties and asks why Israel is dying; Luke warns the hearers that without repentance they too will perish.

This same-chapter refrain repeats the repentance warning after a different tragedy: the tower deaths rather than Pilate's victims. The repeated warning is not independent confirmation of either event.

Both describe fruit sought on a fig tree and not found. Luke tells a parable allowing further time; Matthew narrates Jesus cursing a tree that withers immediately. They are not the same tree or occasion.
Both connect fruitlessness with cutting down a tree. Luke's owner specifies three unsuccessful years; John's warning adds an axe and fire without that period.

Both present delay as opportunity before loss or judgment. Luke's worker seeks another fruit season; Peter names divine patience toward repentance. This comparison does not assign identities to the tree and worker or a timetable to God.
Both condition a tree's removal on failure to produce fruit. Luke allows a further year first; John's warning does not state that delay and adds fire.
Both introduce Sabbath synagogue healing controversies. Luke introduces the bent woman's setting; Mark introduces a man with a withered hand watched by opponents. The patients and events differ.

Luke concretely describes straightening a bent woman who glorifies God; the psalm praises the Lord raising those broken down. The shared raising imagery does not make the psalm name her condition or report her event.
The ruler's appeal to six working days recalls the six-day work and seventh-day Sabbath rule. Exodus does not explicitly prohibit healing, so his contested application is not inserted into the law.
Both defend Sabbath relief through accepted care for animals. Luke cites untying ox or donkey for water; Matthew cites rescuing a sheep from a pit and human worth. The examples differ.

Both argue that human relief is appropriate on the Sabbath. Luke emphasizes Abrahamic identity and release from Satan's eighteen-year bond; Matthew emphasizes human value over a sheep and lawful good.

Both show opponents thwarted after Jesus' Sabbath-healing argument. Luke 13 describes shame and crowd joy; Luke 14 says they cannot answer, without that crowd response. These are different healing scenes.

Luke introduces the kingdom comparison continued as mustard seed in the next verse; Matthew introduces the corresponding seed parable directly. The introduction is read with its continuation, not treated as a separate kingdom image.

Both compare the kingdom to a mustard seed growing into a tree with birds in its branches. Luke describes the birds nesting; Matthew describes them coming and resting. Luke names a garden; Matthew a field and additionally contrasts the seed's smallness with its growth.
Luke introduces a second kingdom comparison whose continuation is leaven; Matthew introduces the corresponding leaven parable in one verse. The question versus statement form remains distinct.
Both compare the kingdom to a woman hiding leaven in three sata of flour until all is leavened. This positive kingdom image is not equated with hypocrisy merely because leaven appears elsewhere.

The later same-book travel notice continues the Jerusalem direction explicitly set earlier. Luke 13 adds teaching through cities and villages; Luke 9 describes the resolve toward His approaching taking-up, not this exact itinerary.
Luke asks whether the saved are few; Matthew contrasts the few finding the narrow life-way with many on the broad destruction-way. Matthew does not repeat the question or give numerical proportions.

Both use a narrow entrance and difficult access to life. Luke says many will seek entry unsuccessfully; Matthew contrasts narrow gate and constricted road with a broad road. Door, gate, and road remain different images.
Both describe a shut door, later appeals Lord, open to us, and refusal because the speaker does not know them. Matthew frames a wedding; Luke a householder, not one identical scene.
Both portray rejected people appealing to association with Jesus. Luke cites eating and teaching in their streets; Matthew cites claimed prophecy and mighty works. The claimed credentials differ.
Both declare lack of recognition and command workers of wrongdoing to depart. Luke adds not knowing their origin and says unrighteousness; Matthew says never knew and lawlessness.
Both contrast being with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom with weeping exclusion. Luke includes all prophets; Matthew names sons of the kingdom and outer darkness.
Both describe people arriving from distant directions to recline in God's kingdom. Luke adds north and south to east and west; Matthew names the patriarchs in that verse.
Both announce reversal of first and last. Luke says there are last who will be first; Matthew says many first will be last, preserving the different formulations.

Both connect Jerusalem with rejection and death of prophets. Luke's rhetorical statement about His destined route is compared with Matthew's lament, not converted into a claim that every prophet historically died only there.
Both lament Jerusalem's killing of prophets and unwillingness to gather under protective wings. Luke says bird and brood; Matthew says hen and chicks.
Both speak of the house being left and future sight of Jesus linked to the Lord-name blessing. Matthew explicitly says desolate; that adjective is absent from Luke's supplied verse.

Both place Jesus at a Pharisee's meal before controversy. Luke 14 specifies a leader's Sabbath meal and close watching; Luke 11 concerns a host's surprise at missing ritual washing. These are different meals.
Both have Jesus ask opponents what is lawful on the Sabbath. Luke asks about healing; Mark contrasts good and evil, saving and killing. The questions precede different patients' healings.

Both report opponents' silence followed by healing. Luke describes taking hold of and dismissing a man with dropsy; Mark describes commanding a withered hand to stretch. The patients and methods differ.
Both appeal to Sabbath rescue from a pit or well. Luke names a son or ox; Matthew names a sheep. The examples and settings are not made identical.
Both report opponents not answering in a Sabbath-healing dispute. Mark's silence follows the initial question; Luke's inability follows the rescue comparison, preserving the different sequence.

Both criticize seeking foremost places at dinners. Luke observes invited guests choosing seats; Matthew describes leaders' love of foremost dinner and synagogue places, without identifying the guest groups as identical.
Both warn against taking a high social place before a more honored person. Luke frames wedding seating; Proverbs warns against placing oneself among rulers and being humbled before them.
Both warn of humiliating demotion when presuming a high place. Luke's host makes the guest yield to another; Proverbs contrasts being invited up with being humbled before a ruler.
Luke's Friend, move up higher recalls Proverbs' preference for being told Come up to me. Luke adds deliberately choosing the lowest seat and honor before fellow guests.
Both state that self-exaltation leads to humiliation and self-humbling to exaltation. The same reversal appears in different teaching settings.

Both reject generosity limited to expected reciprocal benefit. Luke 14 applies it to inviting friends and rich neighbors; Luke 6 applies it to love, doing good, and lending. The specific activities differ.

This same-chapter instruction's poor, disabled, lame, and blind reappear as the banquet parable's invited groups. The repeated list links practical hospitality with the illustration, not an independently reported guest list.
Both connect mercy toward the poor with repayment beyond their resources. Proverbs names God's repayment; Luke specifies the resurrection of the righteous, a timing statement absent from Proverbs.

Both picture eating in God's kingdom. Luke records a guest's blessing on those eating bread there; Matthew's Jesus describes distant arrivals reclining with the patriarchs. The speakers and fuller images differ.
Both introduce a feast host inviting guests. Luke's host is a man giving a great supper; Matthew's is a king arranging his son's wedding, preserving distinct settings.
Both send servants to previously invited people with the announcement that the meal is ready. Luke sends one slave; Matthew describes plural messengers and a renewed invitation.
Both portray a field-related pursuit displacing attendance. Luke's invitee excuses himself to inspect a newly bought field; Matthew says a guest disregards the invitation and goes to his field.

Both contrast business activity with accepting the feast. Luke specifies testing purchased oxen; Matthew merely says business, not this animal purchase. The relationship compares excuses rather than independently confirming the oxen.

Both mention obligations associated with a new marriage. Deuteronomy exempts the new husband from war and imposed duty for a year; Luke records a banquet excuse. The law is not made an exemption from this feast or proof that the excuse is valid.
Both replace refusing invitees with people called from public places. Luke specifies poor and disabled people; Matthew gathers everyone found, evil and good, without Luke's exact list.

Both extend the feast invitation onto roads to fill the banquet. Luke adds fences and compel people to come; Matthew says invite those found. The differing words and rounds of invitation remain distinct.
Both exclude the original invited people after their refusal. Luke says none will taste the supper; Matthew calls those invited unworthy.

Both demand allegiance to Jesus beyond family loyalty. Luke uses hate and includes spouse, siblings, and one's life; Matthew says loving parents or children more than Him. Their wording is not rewritten into identity.
Both require carrying one's cross and following Jesus. Luke says one otherwise cannot be a disciple; Matthew says one is not worthy of Him.

Both connect building with prior readiness. Luke counts expense before building a tower; Proverbs commands work and field preparation before rebuilding a house. Proverbs does not mention Luke's budget calculation or tower.

Both associate warfare with deliberation. Luke's king assesses unequal forces; the supplied Proverbs text speaks of steering war and a deliberative heart. It does not supply Luke's army numbers or a guaranteed outcome.

Both describe seeking terms before battle. Luke's weaker king sends a delegation while the opponent is distant; Deuteronomy's approaching attacker offers peace to a city. The military roles and rules are different.

Both connect relinquishing possessions with following Jesus. Luke makes a general discipleship demand; Matthew directs the wealthy questioner to sell, give to the poor, and follow, with heavenly treasure.
Both call salt good and ask how tasteless salt can be seasoned. Mark additionally commands having salt and peace; Luke continues to disposal.
Both describe useless salt being thrown away. Luke specifies unfitness for soil or manure and adds the hearing summons; Matthew mentions trampling and does not give those uses.
Both depict tax collectors and sinners gathering around Jesus. Luke specifies coming to hear; Matthew describes a shared meal with disciples. The scenes and immediate activities differ.
Both report Pharisaic objections to Jesus eating with sinners. Luke includes scribes and direct grumbling; Matthew has Pharisees question the disciples about their Teacher.

Luke introduces the lost-sheep story following criticism of welcoming sinners; Matthew gives the corresponding illustration with the Father's little ones. The introductory unit is read with its continuation, not as a separate parable.
Both describe one lost sheep out of a hundred and leaving ninety-nine to seek it. Luke says wilderness and until finding; Matthew says mountains and seeking the straying one.
Both join finding the sheep with rejoicing. Luke adds carrying it on the shoulders; Matthew compares the joy with the ninety-nine, without that carrying detail.
The same-chapter stories repeat calling friends and neighbors to rejoice over recovering one lost possession. Here it is a man's sheep; there a woman's coin. The owners and objects remain distinct.
Both make the recovered one an occasion of joy in contrast to ninety-nine. Luke applies it to heavenly joy over repentance; Matthew to the Father's will that no little one perish.

Both same-chapter stories describe an owner seeking one missing item among a known number until found. Luke contrasts a woman's lamp-and-sweeping coin search with the man's wilderness sheep search, not one event.
This repeated same-chapter celebration formula parallels the sheep owner's call to friends and neighbors. The woman rejoices over one drachma rather than one sheep, preserving the different stories.
Both applications state joy over one repentant sinner. Luke 15:10 locates it before God's angels; 15:7 says heaven and adds the comparison with ninety-nine.

Both introduce a father with two children as a parable's framework. Matthew tests responses to a vineyard command; Luke develops inheritance, departure, return, and the older son's response. The plots are not one.

Both adjacent stories use scattering possessions to describe economic loss. Luke 15 narrates the son's reckless spending; Luke 16 reports an accusation against a steward over another's property. The charge and the narrated fact, and the roles, differ.
This same-chapter resolve to rise, go to the father, and confess corresponds to the narrated return and repeated confession. It is a plan-and-action link, not independent attestation.
The planned statement of unworthiness is repeated in the son's recorded confession. The planned hired-worker request is not repeated there; no invented cause for that omission is supplied.

Both family reunions involve running, falling on a neck, and kissing. Genesis describes Esau welcoming his brother Jacob with tears; Luke a compassionate father welcoming his son. The family roles and circumstances remain different.

The actual confession repeats the earlier planned sin acknowledgment and unworthiness. The earlier servant request is absent from the recorded confession, so the two speeches are not declared identical in every clause.

Both dress a favored recipient and give a ring. Luke's father provides robe and sandals to his son; Pharaoh gives Joseph linen and a gold collar. The honors do not make the offices or recipients identical.

Both hosts prepare fattened animals and call for a feast. Luke celebrates a son's return with a calf; Matthew's king announces a wedding meal with bulls and fattened animals. The feasts and sons are not equated.

The same-chapter refrain repeats dead/alive and lost/found as grounds for celebration. The father first says my son and later your brother, emphasizing the family relation without narrating a literal bodily resurrection.

The servant reports completed slaughter of the calf ordered earlier in this chapter. That command-and-report link does not make the earlier order an independent witness to every detail of the servant's explanation.

Both portray resentment of generous treatment of a late or returning recipient. Luke's older son refuses the feast and is entreated by his father; Matthew's earlier workers grumble and receive the owner's reply.
Both complaints contrast the speaker's lengthy labor with favorable treatment of another. Luke cites years of obedient service and no goat; Matthew cites the day's burden and heat versus one hour.

Both resentful speakers present another recipient as less deserving. Luke's brother alleges spending on prostitutes; Matthew's workers cite shorter labor. The brother's allegation is not turned into independent narrator confirmation or the workers' story.

Both benefactors defend generosity while addressing an earlier claimant's rights. Luke's father says his property is the older son's; Matthew's owner honors the agreed wage while freely giving another the same. The property relationships differ.

This same-chapter return to the dead/alive and lost/found refrain repeats the reason for joy. The father now says your brother rather than my son, applying the same restoration to the older son's response.

Both adjacent stories use scattering possessions for economic waste. Luke 16 reports an accusation against a steward over someone else's property; Luke 15 narrates the son's reckless spending. The evidentiary status and family or employment roles differ.

Both portray a master calling entrusted servants to account. Luke's steward faces dismissal after an accusation; Matthew's returning master settles accounts after a long absence. The businesses and preceding events differ.

The steward plans later welcome into houses, while Jesus' application speaks of welcome into eternal tents through friends made with wealth. This internal reception motif contrasts temporal security and the stated application without endorsing fraud or identifying the dwellings as the same.

Both value prudence, but Matthew expressly also requires innocence. Luke's master praises the unrighteous steward specifically for acting prudently; the comparison does not turn that limited commendation into moral approval of his conduct.

Both direct present possessions toward an enduring future. Luke 12 explicitly names alms and heavenly treasure; Luke 16 names friends and eternal tents. The images and instructions are related, not identical transactions.
Both connect faithfulness in little with greater responsibility. Luke also states the negative principle for unrighteousness; Matthew's praise of the faithful slave does not repeat that half.

Both distinguish present money from a more lasting good requiring responsible use. Luke contrasts unrighteous mammon with true riches; Timothy contrasts uncertain wealth with generous good works and truly living. It does not repeat Luke's exact entrustment question.
Both bind stewardship to faithfulness over what is entrusted. Luke asks about another's property and future possession of one's own; Paul names God's mysteries, not the same assets or reward.
Both describe the impossibility of serving two masters, opposite loyalties, and the incompatibility of serving God and mammon.
Both condemn love of money. Luke identifies sneering opponents as money-lovers; Timothy describes love of money's evils and some people's wandering from faith, not the biography of these Pharisees.

Both expose outward righteousness before people concealing inward corruption. Luke names God's knowledge of hearts and human exaltation's divine disapproval; Matthew uses whitewashed tombs, hypocrisy, and lawlessness.

Both place John at a transition involving Law, Prophets, and kingdom. Luke says everyone presses into the proclaimed kingdom; Matthew describes violence and seizure. The expressions are not forced into one interpretation.
Both contrast passing heaven and earth with the Law's enduring smallest written mark. Matthew adds iota and until all is accomplished; Luke names a small stroke falling.

Both connect divorce and remarriage with adultery and mention marrying a divorced woman. Matthew includes a sexual-immorality exception and causing adultery; Luke's supplied sentence does not repeat those qualifications.

Both depict luxurious living within a warning about judgment. Luke specifies purple, linen, and daily splendor; James names indulgence and the slaughter day. James's surrounding accusations are not imported as the rich man's unstated biography.

Both place food falling from a table and dogs in a need-related scene. Matthew's little dogs eat crumbs; Luke's dogs lick Lazarus's sores while he longs for fallen food. The actions and human roles are not equated.

Both depict blessed association with Abraham. Luke describes the dead poor man carried by angels to Abraham's bosom; Matthew describes arrivals reclining with patriarchs in the kingdom. The images are not declared identical.

Both portray distressed exclusion alongside sight of Abraham in blessed company. Luke 13 uses kingdom exclusion and weeping; Luke 16 explicitly names Hades, torment, and Lazarus. The distinct images are not turned into one asserted geography.

Both contrast poor or suffering people's future comfort with rich people's present good followed by reversal. The beatitudes and woes state the pattern generally; the parable applies it to two figures without supplying identical histories.

Both give Moses' words weight as available testimony. Luke's Abraham directs the brothers to hear Moses and Prophets; John's Jesus links belief in Moses' writings with belief in Himself. The speakers and audiences differ.

Luke's rich man proposes a dead visitor as a cause of repentance; John narrates a raising followed by many believing. The parable's beggar and John's Lazarus are not identified from their shared name, and belief is not made a universal response.

Luke rejects resurrection as a guarantee of persuasion when Scripture is ignored; John depicts priests plotting against raised Lazarus while others believe. The response comparison does not identify the beggar with Jesus' Bethany friend.

deferred.reason: The particular request that Jesus compel a brother to divide an inheritance was read. General inheritance rules do not establish this claimant's rights or circumstances, so no independent counterpart was retained.
The rich man's question about insufficient crop storage was read. No sufficiently precise counterpart to that particular deliberation was retained.
The plan to demolish and enlarge storehouses was read. Other accounts of storing grain were not treated as this same demolition-and-rebuilding plan.
The report of Pilate mixing Galileans' blood with their sacrifices was read. No independent biblical account of this specific event was established.
The eighteen tower deaths at Siloam were read. Generic tower or disaster passages do not independently establish this event or its victims.
The bent woman's eighteen-year spirit of weakness was read. Other chronic illnesses do not independently attest this distinctive condition or duration.
The particular call and pronouncement of release to this woman were read. Generic healing pronouncements were not used solely to complete the unit.
The Pharisees' warning that Herod wanted to kill Jesus was read. Other Herod notices were not treated as independent confirmation of this specific warning or its truth.
The fox reply and today/tomorrow/third-day completion wording were read. It was not simply equated with a separately stated resurrection timetable or a generic healing summary.
The man with dropsy was read. Other sick men or Sabbath healings do not independently attest this distinct illness and appearance.
The servant's statement that the order was completed while room remained was read. The different banquet story's final fullness was not retained as an exact counterpart to this progress report.
The traveling crowd and Jesus' turning to address it were read. Generic crowd and travel transitions were not used to manufacture a counterpart.
The unfinished foundation and resulting mockery were read. Mockery of other building projects does not establish this precise failure from insufficient resources.
The spectators' statement about beginning but not finishing was read. No sufficiently precise independent counterpart was retained.
The younger son's demand and the father's division of livelihood were read. A presumed legal share, firstborn ratio, or identical family dispute was not supplied from general inheritance passages.
The famine after the son's spending was read. Other famines do not independently attest these circumstances or establish the same country.
The son's employment feeding pigs was read. Purity laws about eating pork were not represented as an explicit law about this job, and unrelated herdsmen do not establish his identity.
The carob-pod hunger and nobody giving him anything were read. No sufficiently precise separate counterpart was retained.
The internal comparison of the father's workers' bread with his hunger was read. General bread or hunger sayings were not treated as this particular realization.
The older son hearing music and dancing on returning from the field was read. Other musical scenes do not establish this distinctive approach to the house.
The older son's question to a servant was read. Generic questions about noises or crowds were not retained as close counterparts.
The steward's private deliberation about digging and begging after dismissal was read. Generic economic worries do not repeat this particular dilemma.
The calling of the master's debtors and first debt question were read. No precise independent counterpart to this negotiation was retained.
The hundred-to-fifty oil-document revision was read. A theory about removing interest or commission was not invented, and other debts do not independently establish these figures.
The hundred-to-eighty wheat-document revision was read. No unverified commercial explanation or independent validation of these figures was supplied.
Lazarus's poverty, gateway location, and sores were read. General sore-covered sufferers were not treated as this figure or a sufficiently precise separate account.
The plea for a wet finger to cool the tongue in flame was read. Generic thirst or fire texts were not retained as an exact counterpart to this distinctive request.
The fixed, uncrossable chasm was read. No independent matching passage was established, and extra geography was not added.
The request to send Lazarus to the father's house was read. No independent counterpart to this particular proposed visit was retained.
The five brothers and requested warning were read. They were not assigned names, historical relatives, or a symbolic identification without evidence.

review_notes: All 192 actual Luke 12–16 source units and all retained targets were read from the exact Saints snapshots with context. The proposed 162 paired sources have 162 distinct pairs; 30 sources remain deferred with zero completion credit.

Every relationship has an individual explanation. Distinct settings, speakers, roles, monetary details, images, and differing narrated versus alleged actions remain explicit. The initial pass is selective rather than an exhaustive concordance.

Same-book links explicitly identify recurring teaching, parable motifs, mirrored speeches, planned-and-reported fulfillment, and deliberate refrains. They do not provide independent witnesses or turn adjacent accounts into the same event.

Sirach 11:18–19 is compared with the rich-fool story's wealth, rest, enjoyment, uncertain lifespan, and goods left to others; it does not supply Luke's agricultural yield, storehouse demolition, or this-night timing.

The Sabbath ruler's six-working-days argument is compared with Exodus without making Exodus explicitly forbid healing. Other Sabbath controversies retain different patients, actions, examples, and response sequences.

Proverbs comparisons use the actual Saints wording, including 24:6's steering and deliberative heart and 24:27's field preparation and rebuilding. Neither passage is silently rewritten with a familiar alternative edition's wording.

Banquet parallels preserve king versus ordinary householder, wedding versus supper, servants' numbers, named versus unspecified excuses, guest categories, and differing invitation words. The new-marriage duty exemption does not establish a legal exemption from the parable's feast.

The return of the younger son preserves narration versus the older brother's allegation about prostitutes. No cause is invented for omission of the planned hired-worker request from the recorded confession. Dead/alive restoration language is not automatically made a literal bodily resurrection.

The steward is accused of scattering another's possessions; the son is narrated scattering his own. The master's commendation is expressly about prudence and does not erase the description unrighteous or endorse dishonest transactions.

No speculative interest-rate, commission, inheritance-share, or historical-family theory is used to explain unique figures or people. Unknown five brothers are not identified with an actual family or a symbolic set.

Luke's parable Lazarus and John's Bethany Lazarus remain distinct figures. John's resurrection and mixed responses are compared with the parable's proposed miracle argument without inferring identity from a repeated name.
Hades, Abraham's bosom, kingdom exclusion, and other judgment images retain their wording and settings. The record adds no afterlife geography or identification of the fixed chasm with another place.

Target IDs, contiguous original ranges, complete source coverage, unique directed pairs, and exclusion of self targets are checked against the pinned originals before acceptance. Original wording, gaps, and continuation paragraphs remain unchanged.
This is AI-assisted English passage review, not exhaustive concordance, fresh Greek apparatus approval, independent human specialist review, or live destination-anchor verification.
